object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account; everything hangs off it. Represents a customer for billing purposes.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.

object_types.name: Account Number
object_types.definition: Six-digit, sequential identifier for an account, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a given amount on a given cycle for a given product, identified by a subscription ID.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product sold by the company, identified by a product code. Three today: CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: Price Plan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that says what the customer pays and how often; generates the invoice line.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.
And I mean the billing artefact. The thing that generates the invoice line.

object_types.name: Feature Bundle
object_types.definition: The feature bundle a customer gets - what they get (seats, API, SSO); the thing on the pricing page. Identified by name.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO. It's the thing on the pricing page.
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me. ... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: Start Date
object_types.definition: The date a subscription begins; always present.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: End Date
object_types.definition: The date a subscription ends; optional, present only for fixed-term subscriptions or after cancellation.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front, that's usually an enterprise deal.

object_types.name: Billing Period
object_types.definition: The billing cycle of a subscription: monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual.

object_types.name: Subscription Status
object_types.definition: The status of a subscription: trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

object_types.name: Paused Flag
object_types.definition: A separate boolean flag indicating a subscription is paused; not a status value, though it behaves like one and overlaps confusingly with status.

source_references.excerpt: There's also paused. ... Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

object_types.name: MRR
object_types.definition: Monthly recurring revenue; derived value, computed from price plan price normalised to a month and billing period, not stored as an asserted fact.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR. Monthly recurring revenue. It's the number I live in.
It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month. An annual plan at 490 is an MRR of 40.83.

object_types.name: Plan Change
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, with its own identity, effective date, requester, and the new price plan.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date, and the subscription's current plan is derived from the change history. ... It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: Effective Date
object_types.definition: The date on which a plan change takes effect, which may differ from the date the change was made.

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person who requested a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.
Subscription ID. The account. The product. The price plan. Start date. End date, sometimes. Billing period. Status.

ambiguities.description: The word 'plan' is used for at least three distinct concepts: the billing artefact (Price Plan), the feature bundle customers get (Feature Bundle), and a sales-negotiated deal ('what the sales team calls a plan'). The transcript explicitly leaves the sales-deal concept out of scope ('That's a different meeting'), so it's unclear whether it needs modeling or is truly out of scope.

source_references.excerpt: So we've got two things both called plan. ... We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.
Only that we still call three different things "plan" and this document won't fix that.

ambiguities.description: Whether 'one active subscription per account per product' is enforced as a hard database constraint or could be violated is stated firmly, but the exact mechanics of what counts as 'active' (interacting with the separate 'paused' flag) are unclear, since paused subscriptions are reported as active by some system queries.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: The commercial/business rule for mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions (run to term vs prorated refund vs credit) is explicitly undecided and parked; only the current system behavior (end date set to paid-through date, no refund mechanism) is captured. The four manual refunds given are ambiguous as to whether they represent an emerging unwritten policy or true exceptions.

source_references.excerpt: Four times in a quarter isn't goodwill, it's a policy nobody's written down. ... What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided.

ambiguities.description: There is a discrepancy about whether the subscription has a stored 'current price plan' field or whether the current plan is purely derived from plan change history; this was corrected mid-conversation (Sam initially says it's derived, then Priya clarifies there IS a denormalised current plan field maintained by the change process, and Sam withdraws his correction). The exact authoritative source of truth in case of disagreement (change history wins) is stated, but the reliability/maintenance mechanism of the denormalised field is only lightly described.

source_references.excerpt: One correction. You said a subscription belongs to one price plan. It doesn't, really -- that's what the plan changes are for. ... No, Sam, it does have a current plan field. ... Correct. And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: The fourth product 'in discovery' is mentioned but explicitly not yet defined or named, leaving the Product object type's population as fixed at three today but potentially incomplete.

source_references.excerpt: Fixed at three? ... Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: It's unclear whether 'Requester' should be modeled as a full entity type (e.g., linked to Account/Contact/Employee) or just as a simple text/name value, since the transcript only says a plan change records 'who requested it' without further identification detail.

source_references.excerpt: It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

ambiguities.description: The 'quarterly' billing period existed for one customer historically but was bought out; it's unclear whether this should be modeled as a historical value ever in the value constraint or excluded entirely, since the current rule is 'only those two' (monthly/annual).

source_references.excerpt: Only those two. There was a quarterly once, for one customer, and it caused so much trouble that we bought them out of it.
